## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Thusajātaka* (Ja 338) is a story included in the Pali Jātaka collection. The narrative was delivered by the Buddha while residing at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana) in Rājagaha, occasioned by Prince Ajātasattu [Fausböll 1883]. The background narrative (*paccupannavatthu*) recounts that during Ajātasattu's conception, his pregnant mother experienced an abnormal craving (*dohada*) to drink blood from the right knee of her husband, King Bimbisāra [Wu 2012; Radich 2011a]. Foretellers prophesied that the unborn child would become the murderer of his father [Wu 2012; Radich 2011b].

In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher (*disāpāmokkha ācariya*) at Takkasilā who provided verses to a royal pupil, enabling the king to discern danger and foil repeated assassination attempts orchestrated by his patricidal son [Fausböll 1883; Radich 2011a]. The opening verse (*gāthā*) highlights how mice can distinguish chaff from grain even in total darkness, discarding the husk (*thusa*) to eat the rice grain (*taṇḍula*) (*Viditaṁ thusaṁ undurānaṁ, viditaṁ pana taṇḍulaṁ...*) [Fausböll 1883]. Modern scholarship has noted the role of this Jātaka's distinctive mother-son motifs and prenatal prophecies in the broader development and comparative reception of the Ajātaśatru narrative tradition [Wu 2012; Radich 2011a; Harding et al. 2015].

According to DharmaNexus alignments, the canonical text shares substantial segments with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* and shows machine-detected parallels with Kṣemendra's Tibetan translation of the *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā* [DharmaNexus].
